cards.headline: A loan you can trade.
cards.body: Buy a bond and you are the lender, not the owner. A government or company borrows your money and owes it back, with interest, on a set date. Unlike a personal loan, you can sell that claim to someone else at any time.

art.alt: A lender hands coins to a company building and receives a folded note with a calendar marker — a loan that comes back with interest on a set date.

cards.headline: Three numbers define it.
cards.body: A bond is described by three things. The **face value** is the amount repaid at the end. The **coupon** is the yearly interest in dollars. The **maturity** is the date the face value comes back. Everything else follows from these.

cards.title: Owner versus lender

art.name: equity-vs-debt
art.alt: A shareholder stands inside the business as an owner; a bondholder stands outside holding an IOU to be repaid first.

cards.caption: A shareholder owns a piece of the company and its ups and downs. A bondholder simply lent money and is owed a fixed sum back — a different seat, a different risk.

cards.headline: The coupon rate is simple division.
cards.body: The coupon rate is the yearly interest divided by the face value. A bond with a **$1,000** face paying a **$50** coupon has a coupon rate of **5%**. That rate is fixed for the life of the bond and never changes.

cards.prompt: A company goes bankrupt. Who has the stronger claim to be paid: a bondholder or a shareholder?

options.label: The bondholder — debt is paid first

cards.explanation: Lenders are paid before owners. Bondholders are creditors, so they stand ahead of shareholders when a failing company is broken up. That seniority is why a bond is usually less risky than the same company's stock.

cards.headline: The appeal is knowing.
cards.body: A bond's draw is predictability. You know the interest you will receive and the date your money returns. A stock promises neither. For income now, or money needed on a known future date, that certainty is the whole point.

cards.headline: Predictable is not risk-free.
cards.body: The promise is only as good as the borrower. A shaky company can fail to pay and default. That is why a risky borrower must offer a higher coupon to attract lenders — the extra interest is the price of the extra risk.
A bond's coupon rate is the yearly interest divided by its [[1]] value, and it stays fixed for the whole life of the bond.
cards.explanation: Face value is the sum repaid at maturity, and the coupon is quoted against it. A $50 coupon on a $1,000 face is a fixed 5% coupon rate for the bond's entire life.

cards.summary: A bond is a tradable loan with a fixed coupon and a set repayment date, ranking ahead of stock.
bullets: Face, coupon and maturity are the three defining numbers.
Coupon rate = yearly coupon ÷ face value.
Bondholders are paid before shareholders if the issuer fails.

art.alt: A lender hands coins to a company building and receives a folded note with a calendar marker — a loan that comes back with interest on a set date.

cards.insight: A shareholder owns the upside and the risk. A bondholder just wants to be paid back — less to gain, and first in line.
